Exhaustive

/ig-ZAW-stiv/ — stress on ZAW · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something exhaustive covers every possible detail or option, leaving nothing out.

The committee ran an exhaustive check of every bolt on the roller coaster.

Worked Example

The detective's exhaustive review of the surveillance footage revealed every second of the suspect's movements that night.

Exhaust + -ive: Exhaust means to use up completely or deplete. The -ive suffix means 'having the quality of, inclined to.' So exhaustive = having the quality of using something up completely. In analysis and search contexts, this means a review that uses up every possibility or detail, leaving nothing out. This decomposition reveals why exhaustive doesn't mean tiring — that's exhausting, a different adjective from the same verb.

How Exhaustive Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

Antonyms

cursory

superficial

How Strong Is It? — careful → thorough → comprehensive → exhaustive

careful vs. exhaustive

careful vs. exhaustive: A careful review checks the important parts; an exhaustive one checks absolutely everything.

thorough vs. exhaustive

thorough vs. exhaustive: 'Thorough' means well done with attention, but exhaustive means no detail, option, or corner was left unexamined.

comprehensive vs. exhaustive

comprehensive vs. exhaustive: A comprehensive report covers all the main areas; an exhaustive one leaves nothing out at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — exhaust

Root — exhaust: to drain, use up completely — from Latin exhaurire, 'to draw out, drain' (Latin)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: having the quality or tendency of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Exhaust + -ive: having the quality of using something up completely — a search or list so thorough it exhausts every single possibility.

Use the root in a new word: inexhaustible

Use the root in a new word: inexhaustible: The toddler's supply of energy seemed inexhaustible right up until bedtime.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Reach for exhaustive when describing a review, search, or analysis that covers every possible detail or option with nothing left out. For everyday contexts, thorough is simpler. Exhaustive is stronger and implies absolute completeness. Key distinction: exhausting uses the same root but is a different word entirely.
